newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Senior U.N. official warns against free market.
newsitem.headline: Senior U.N. official warns against free market.

text.p: A senior U.N. official warned on Wednesday that leaving world economic development to an unfettered free market would widen the gap between rich and poor and bring a global backlash that could wreck reform.

Rubens Ricupero, Secretary-General of the U.N. Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), also accused major powers of pushing developing countries to open their economies while keeping home markets firmly protected against their goods.
"Globalisation is a fact of life, one that cannot be wished away," the former Brazilian finance minister told a meeting in Geneva of the world body's Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC).

"But it would be a great error to assume that, in consequence, market forces must be given untrammelled free rein," he said. The role of governments would be even more crucial in the next century than in the past.

The UNCTAD chief, who played key role in moving the agency towards a liberal economic stance from the more left- wing views it once espoused, visibly surprised some of his audience with the fervour of his remarks.

"If globalisation is to deserve its name, it has to include, not to exclude, to integrate and not to marginalise," he said in a reference to the process of integrating the world economy by liberalising trade and lowering barriers for services like banking and telecommunications.

"If some recent trends end up by causing social disintegration inside countries and pushing nations and continents to the periphery of history, then globalisation will have betrayed its promise, and its very name.
"If there is one indisputable lesson of history, it is that no economic law exists that will make the incomes of developing countries converge automatically towards those of developed countries."

Ricupero's remarks clearly reflected a growing sense of concern among emerging economies against what they see as pressure, especially from the United States, to use the World Trade Organisation (WTO) to force open their markets.

Governments in poorer states "share the perception that trade is being seen by some developed countries as a means of global governance...They fear a continuous pressure to expand the frontiers of the multi-lateral trading system," he said.

Ricupero drew a gloomy world social picture, noting that growth had been too slow to generate jobs or cut poverty, that wage inequality between skilled and unskilled was a global trend and that the middle classes were everywhere being squeezed.

His speech contrasted with an address by Renato Ruggiero, who became head of the then fledgling WTO two years ago and is a vociferous advocate of globalisation and an end to trade barriers.
Ruggiero said more needed to be done to help the poorest countries but he argued they would also best help themselves by further liberalising their economies.

He said globalisation would not solve the problems of income distribution but it provided "the most powerful engine for growth the world has yet seen -- an essential basis for building the shared global society that is now within our reach."
